candidate.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — therapeutic communication adapted to a client with post-stroke aphasia
candidate.educational_objective: Communicate with a client who has post-stroke aphasia by allowing time and using clear adult-level language plus individualized multimodal supports without assuming cognitive incapacity.

options.A: Use short adult-level sentences, speak at a comfortable pace and volume, allow extra response time, and use writing, pictures, or gestures when helpful.
options.B: Speak loudly and rapidly so the client receives more information before becoming frustrated by the communication difficulty.
options.C: Direct questions primarily to the family because aphasia indicates that the client is unable to understand spoken language or participate in decisions.
options.D: Avoid alternative communication methods so the client must practice spoken language during every interaction until verbal fluency returns.

candidate.rationale: ASHA guidance for adults with communication disorders recommends simple but adult language, slower speech, short sentences, adequate time to communicate, and multimodal supports such as pictures, writing, and gestures when useful. Aphasia does not automatically imply cognitive impairment or absent comprehension. Therefore, A is best. B adds unnecessary loudness and speed, C wrongly assumes incapacity and bypasses the client, and D removes compensatory communication methods that can support effective participation.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Directly supports adult-level simplified language, appropriate pace/volume, extra response time, multimodal communication supports, and avoidance of the assumption that aphasia means cognitive incapacity.
candidate.source_document_title: Aphasia — ASHA Practice Portal; Tips for Communicating With Adults Who Have a Speech or Language Disorder
candidate.source_locator: ASHA Practice Portal → Aphasia → Differential Diagnosis: aphasia does not imply cognitive deficits; Partner Approaches → Conversational Coaching and Supported Conversation for Adults With Aphasia: communication partners may use drawing, gesturing, cueing, confirming, summarizing and multimodal communication. ASHA communication tips → 'To help someone understand you better': keep voice at a comfortable level, use simple but adult words, slow speech, short sentences, and pictures/gestures/writing; 'To help someone express themselves better': give time to communicate and invite drawing, writing, pointing, or gesturing as needed.
